newsitem.title: USA: US SUGAR IMPORT QUOTA HOLDERS WORRIED ABOUT MEXICO.
newsitem.headline: US SUGAR IMPORT QUOTA HOLDERS WORRIED ABOUT MEXICO.

text.p: Mexico's privileged access to the U.S. sugar market is weighing heavily on the minds of other exporters as U.S. Agriculture Department faces its annual task of determining how much imported sugar to allow.

In comments filed with USDA, the exporters said they were worried about reports that the U.S. and Mexico are engaged in negotiations that might guarantee Mexico an even larger share of the import quota than it currently enjoys.
Some even expressed concern that Cuba, under U.S. economic embargo since the early 1960s, could one day regain access to the sugar market on a preferential basis.

"If the U.S. makes a special deal with Mexico, it will set the precedent for doing the same with Cuba, which would probably kill the program," Caribbean and Central American nations said in their comments.

"We believe it would be a break of faith to give Mexico access beyond that provided by NAFTA" because many Caribbean and Central American "either entered or increased production at the request of the U.S. government after the embargoed was placed on Cuba," the countries said.
Similar concerns were also expressed in comments filed by Dominican Republic's Sugar Policy Commission, South African Sugar Association and Mauritius Sugar Syndicate.
So far, there seems to be more interest in Mexico in increasing its access to the U.S. sugar market than there is in the United States.
While Mexican officials have raised the issue, it's not something U.S. negotiators have jumped on, a USDA aide said.

Under the North American Free Trade Agreement, Mexico is allowed to ship 25,000 tonnes of either refined or raw sugar to the U.S. -- or slightly more than triple its pre-NAFTA allocation -- in years when it has a sugar surplus.
That was the case in the fiscal 1997 quota year that ends September 30. In addition, Mexico's access under NAFTA increases to 250,000 tonnes in fiscal 2001.

The rest of the U.S. annual import quota is divided among about 40 countries based on their share of the U.S. market between 1976 to 1982. That was the last time U.S. sugar imports were not controlled by a quota.

Under that system, Dominican Republic receives the largest share, or about 17.6 percent. Caribbean and Central American nations, including the Dominican Republic, jointly share about 36.4 percent of the quota. Other large quota holders include Brazil and the Philippines.
Many of those country's economies are heavily dependent on sugar, so granting Mexico a larger share of the annual import quota could have a destabilizing effect on them.

In its comments, Dominican Republic Sugar Policy Commission said it had seen or heard reports "that Mexico may have acquired as much as 300,000 metric tonnes of raw sugar, now in storage, which Mexican sugar importers would like to ship to the U.S. under the quota."

If that is the case, Mexico might try to "make a deal involving increased accessed for this sugar in exchange for the Mexican government" not pursuing a "dumping case" against imports of U.S. high-fructose corn syrup, the commission said.
"Any such deal would be totally inappropriate," the commission said.
In a recent letter to the Sugar Policy Commission, U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman addressed some of the group's concerns.

He noted that few expected Mexico to become a net surplus sugar producer so quickly after the start of NAFTA or the United States to import more than 1.117 million tonnes of raw sugar annually--which was its minimum committment under the 1994 Uruguay Round world trade pact.

"Today, however, we are importing 2.1 million tonnes and Mexico is exporting several hundred thousand tonnes of sugar," Glickman said. "Considering those factors, it becomes very clear why the Mexican producers are asking their government to negotiate additional access to the U.S. market."
Nonetheless, the U.S. has no plans to "deviate from the established NAFTA" provisions governing Mexico's share of the U.S. sugar quota, Glickman said.
"However, we hold out the possibility that we may be able to improve the sugar provisions in the NAFTA for our domestic producers and refiners," he said.
That last point may be easier said than done.
In general, U.S. domestic producers are opposed to any growth in the sugar quota, while U.S. cane refiners would like to see more imports allowed and shipments from Mexico limited to raw product.
USDA has set a Sept 17 deadline for announcing its decision on fiscal 1998 sugar quota. But a decision could come as early as late August, USDA aides have said.
